frameworks.name: Friendship Transactionalism
frameworks.definition: A framework for evaluating friendships based on mutual return on investment rather than emotional obligation or duration, with explicit criteria for inclusion and removal.

frameworks.name: Seasonal Friendships
frameworks.definition: A model treating friendships as time-bound relationships aligned with shared goals; when trajectories diverge, the relationship ends without resentment or obligation.

frameworks.name: Competitive Status Threat Mechanism
frameworks.definition: The dynamic wherein a friend's rising status creates relative status loss for peer group members, incentivizing sabotage through gossip, distraction, and guilt-framing rather than celebration.

claims.text: Alex Hormozi defines friendship not as binary (friends or not friends) but as a gradient: the opposite of friend is an enemy or rival who actively tries to destroy your efforts, make you emotional rather than logical, and distract you from your goal.
claims.speaker: Alex Hormozi

claims.text: A true friend roots for you both in front of you and, more importantly, behind your back; rooting for you behind your back is one of the hardest behaviors in peer groups because rising status creates relative threat to others.
claims.speaker: Alex Hormozi
claims.mechanism: When your status rises, you diminish everyone else's relative status, creating competitive incentive for sabotage through gossip, distraction, and emotional manipulation.
bounded_by: Especially true in alpha-competitive male peer groups

claims.text: Alex Hormozi treats friendship as investment: you allocate time and energy expecting positive return, and the quality of your network depends on investing in relationships with the highest yields.
claims.speaker: Alex Hormozi

claims.text: For Hormozi, the core criterion for keeping a friendship is whether the relationship produces net positive returns: your life is better off with this person in it, they help you achieve your goal, and they root for you. Relationships where this is not true should end.
claims.speaker: Alex Hormozi
conditions: Relationship has measurable impact on goal achievement
bounded_by: Does not apply to obligatory relationships (family, spouse) where long-term alignment is assumed

claims.text: Abundant exchange in relationships occurs when both parties feel they are getting the better end of the deal; such relationships sustain indefinitely with no reason to end them.
claims.speaker: Alex Hormozi
conditions: Both parties perceive they are receiving greater value than giving
claims.mechanism: Mutual positive perceived ROI removes termination pressure and creates compounding reinvestment.

claims.text: When faced between a hard thing and an easy thing and uncertain which to choose, do the hard thing because if the easy thing were correct, you would have already done it.
claims.speaker: Alex Hormozi

claims.text: People do not want the best for you; they want the version of you that serves them best. The closer their long-term alignment to yours, the more likely the two versions overlap, which is why family and spouse relationships have potential for greatest alignment.
claims.speaker: Alex Hormozi
conditions: Relationship between two people with different life trajectories
claims.mechanism: Self-interest drives preference for stable versions of friends; long-term interdependence creates overlapping interest zones.

claims.text: Many people use statements like 'you've changed' to frame your personal growth as a mistake and keep you in your old identity; the appropriate response is 'you're right, and you haven't' because some people prefer to stay the same.
claims.speaker: Alex Hormozi
conditions: Friend expresses discomfort with your growth

claims.text: Friendships naturally have seasons; very few 85-year-olds maintain the same friend group their entire lives. When train tracks align seasonally and then diverge, the relationship ending is natural and acceptable without resentment.
claims.speaker: Alex Hormozi
conditions: Significant life trajectory divergence or goal misalignment
bounded_by: A seasonal friendship does not become an enemy relationship; mutual respect for the shared season persists

claims.text: True help comes from someone who enters your life and makes everything easier; conversely, someone who 'tries to help' but makes your life 10 times harder is destruction, not help.
claims.speaker: Alex Hormozi

claims.text: Removing a friend from your inner circle is not 'burning a bridge' but 'pruning a tree to help it grow'; a tree with limited sunlight, water, and soil nutrients benefits from branch removal even though it feels uncomfortable.
claims.speaker: Alex Hormozi
conditions: Friend relationship no longer aligns with vision or goals

claims.text: When old friends want to keep you in your former identity (clubs, drinking, bar crawls) and you've moved toward new goals, the friendship conflict arises because they're losing access to you, not because you've done something wrong.
claims.speaker: Alex Hormozi
conditions: Significant divergence in lifestyle or goals between friends
claims.mechanism: Friends benefit from status quo; your evolution reduces their access and status connection, creating pressure to maintain old identity.

claims.text: Hormozi uses Tupac's framework: 'Just because you lost me as a friend doesn't mean you gained me as an enemy. I'm bigger than that. I still want to see you eat, just not at my table.' This allows friendship dissolution without animosity.
claims.speaker: Alex Hormozi

claims.text: In hard conversations, keeping the other person as a human being at the forefront rather than focusing on being right produces dramatically better conversation outcomes.
claims.speaker: Alex Hormozi
claims.mechanism: Framing conversation around humanity rather than winning reduces defensive escalation and preserves relationship dignity.

claims.text: You can have friends who aren't pursuing greatness as long as they're helping you pursue yours; the person should inspire you or have something admirable you want to learn from.
claims.speaker: Alex Hormozi
conditions: Friend adds value through inspiration, skill demonstration, or complementary expertise
bounded_by: Friend does not actively sabotage or resent your success

claims.text: Hormozi's core friendship criterion is: Does this person make me better? If not, they have no reason to be in your life.
claims.speaker: Alex Hormozi

claims.text: Extreme views on friendship make sense for people with high demands on their time (multiple people vying for every minute of their day); for those without such constraints, Hormozi's views may not be relevant.
claims.speaker: Alex Hormozi
conditions: High time scarcity due to multiple parties competing for attention
bounded_by: Does not apply to people with ample free time and low external demands

claims.text: Hormozi has built new levels of friends at each achievement level, confirming his prediction that achieving goals unlocks access to higher-caliber peer groups.
claims.speaker: Alex Hormozi

claims.text: The biggest issue with friendships is that people project their own beliefs about what friendship should look like onto the relationship; for transactional friends like Hormozi, incompatible definitions predict friendship incompatibility.
claims.speaker: Alex Hormozi
conditions: Friend holds different mental model of friendship than you

examples.text: Hormozi has one very close friend who is an FBI agent. Every conversation with this friend yields new stories of accomplishments. The mutual benefit is asymmetric: the FBI agent gains nothing financially from Hormozi's status or followers, but both benefit because they're both committed to excellence in their craft. Neither is pursuing the other's industry success but both admire the other's mastery.

When Hormozi achieved his goals, new caliber of friends unlocked at higher success levels. This confirmed his theory that as you achieve and grow, you gain access to better-aligned peer groups naturally.

LeBron James uses 'no new friends' as his rule, having decided he doesn't need or trust new friendships. This works for him because he has a rare life with rare constraints; applying his rules to normal lives would be inappropriate.

practices.text: When decreasing frequency of communication with someone, let the relationship fizzle naturally through fewer invites rather than having an explicit break.
In hard friendship conversations, explicitly acknowledge your own change and frame it as coming from you, not from the other person: 'I've changed and that's not on you, that's on me.'
When friends criticize you for changing, respond with acceptance of their preference to stay the same rather than defensive justification of your growth.
